text: A valid CDF must pass every test in Theorem 4.1: the endpoint limits, continuity, and never decreasing. The slope of a CDF is its PDF [p. 124], so the last test is a sign check on the derivative \(F_T'(t)\).

name: CDF properties for any random variable
text: For any random variable \(X\), (a) \(F_X(-\infty) = 0\), (b) \(F_X(\infty) = 1\), (c) \(P[x_1 < X \le x_2] = F_X(x_2) - F_X(x_1)\).

title: Read the limit off the definition

text: The function is defined to be zero on the whole left half-line \(t < 0\). Approaching \(-\infty\) means traveling left through that region only, so the limit is just the value there.
This is exactly what Theorem 4.1(a) demands: going from left to right, a CDF starts at zero [p. 77].

label: (a)
text: Yes. \(F_T(t) = 0\) for all \(t < 0\), so \(F_T(-\infty) = 0\), as Theorem 4.1(a) requires.
For large \(t\) the leading term \(t^2\) controls both the numerator and the denominator. Dividing both by \(t^2\) shows what survives in the limit.
Numerical sanity check: at \(t = 10^6\), \(F_T(t) = \frac{1000001000000}{1000000000001}\), a hair above 1 and creeping down toward it.

label: (b)
text: Yes. \(\lim_{t \to \infty} F_T(t) = \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{1 + 1/t}{1 + 1/t^2} = 1\), as Theorem 4.1(b) requires.

title: Compare the value and the two one-sided limits

text: The formula changes at \(t = 0\): zero on the left, the rational expression on the right. Continuity there needs the left limit, the right limit, and the value \(F_T(0)\) to agree.

steps.why: \(t = 0\) belongs to \([0, \infty)\), so use the rational branch.
The rational branch is continuous at 0, since \(t^2 + 1 \ge 1 > 0\) never lets the denominator vanish.

name: Continuous random variable
text: \(X\) is a continuous random variable if the CDF \(F_X(x)\) is a continuous function.

Because \(t^2 + 1 \ge 1\), the rational branch is continuous on all of \([0, \infty)\), and \(t = 0\) is the only seam where the two pieces meet. So \(F_T\) is continuous everywhere, which is what Definition 4.2 would demand of a CRV. This test is passed; the trouble comes later.

label: (c)
text: Yes. \(F_T(0) = 0\) and both one-sided limits equal 0, so \(F_T\) is continuous at \(t = 0\) (in fact, everywhere).

Theorem 3.2(b) says a CDF never decreases as it goes from left to right [p. 77], and page 121 confirms these key CDF properties apply to all random variables. To test the rise of \(F_T\), differentiate it: the slope of the CDF is its PDF [p. 124].

name: PDF properties
text: For a continuous random variable \(X\) with PDF \(f_X(x)\), (a) \(f_X(x) \ge 0\) for all \(x\), (b) \(F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(u)\,du\), (c) \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x)\,dx = 1\).

steps.why: Quotient rule on the rational branch, which is the piece of \(F_T\) that lives on \(t \ge 0\).
Expand and collect: the \(2t^3\) terms cancel.

text: Check the expansion at \(t = 3\): the direct form gives \((2\cdot 3+1)(3^2+1) - (3^2+3)(2\cdot 3) = -2\), and the simplified numerator gives \(-3^2 + 2\cdot 3 + 1 = -2\).

title: Find where the slope turns negative

text: The denominator \((t^2+1)^2\) is positive for every \(t\), so the sign of \(f_T\) is the sign of its numerator, which can only flip where the numerator is zero.

steps.why: The minus root \(1 - \sqrt{2} \approx -0.414\) is negative, outside the range of \(T\).
Past the crossover the numerator is negative, so the PDF is negative.

title: A negative PDF is impossible
text: Theorem 4.2(a) requires \(f_X \ge 0\), and its proof says exactly why: \(F_X\) is nondecreasing, so its derivative cannot be negative [p. 125]. Here \(f_T < 0\) for \(t > 1 + \sqrt{2}\): \(F_T\) climbs to a peak of about 1.20711 at \(t \approx 2.41421\) and then falls back toward 1. A CDF can never come back down.

title: Pin the failure on two points

text: No calculus is needed to see the drop once you know where to look. Compare two points past the peak.

steps.why: The CDF dropped as \(t\) moved right, which Theorem 3.2(b) forbids [p. 77].

title: Watch the equal pair
text: It is tempting to compare \(t = 2\) and \(t = 3\), but \(F_T(2) = F_T(3) = 6/5\). Equal values do not violate nondecreasing, since the property allows flat stretches. The violation needs a strict drop, which the pair \(5/2 \to 3\) provides.

There is a second, independent failure. Since \(F_T(1) = 1\), and \(F_T(2) = 6/5 > 1\), the function exceeds 1 for \(t > 1\). A CDF value is a probability, \(F_X(x) = P[X \le x]\) [p. 77], so it can never be larger than 1.

title: F_T(t) climbs past 1, peaks near t = 2.41, then falls back

text: The plot is secondary evidence only, as the problem allows. The sign of \(f_T\) and the two-point comparison above stand on their own, with no reference to the picture.

The verdict: three of the four requirements pass, but monotonicity fails, so \(F_T\) is **not** a valid CDF for any random variable, continuous or otherwise. A function that comes back down would assign negative probability to some interval via \(P[x_1 < X \le x_2] = F_X(x_2) - F_X(x_1)\) [p. 121], and a function that rises above 1 would assign probability greater than 1. Both are impossible.
